title: Infrastructure-Led Urban Transformation and Residential Relocation: Assessing Socio-Spatial Impacts on Coastal Communities
content: Large-scale transportation infrastructure can improve regional connectivity and stimulate urban development, but its social consequences are often unevenly distributed among affected communities. This study examines the socio-spatial implications of infrastructure-led urban transformation through the Al Batinah Coastal Road project in Barka, Oman, focusing on residential relocation, compensation, coastal livelihoods, and community relationships. A mixed-methods case study combined 104 valid questionnaire responses, 15 semi-structured resident interviews, consultations with government officials, documentary review, and field observations. Descriptive analysis identified strong public support for the road’s anticipated contribution to regional connectivity (90.4%), coastal development (84.6%), and investment value (80.8%). However, evaluations of relocation outcomes were more mixed. While 68.3% of respondents considered compensation residential areas adequately planned and serviced, only 37.5% regarded compensation as fair and reasonable, and 41.4% preferred living in the new residential areas. Respondents also reported changes in everyday lifestyles and coastal activities, with fishing households describing reduced convenience in accessing boats and equipment. Perceptions of disrupted social relationships further highlighted the importance of neighbourhood ties beyond dwelling quality. The findings reveal a distinction between anticipated regional development benefits and household-level experiences of spatial restructuring. They underscore the need to integrate livelihood accessibility, transparent compensation, community participation, and post-relocation monitoring into infrastructure planning. Such measures are particularly important in coastal settlements where livelihoods depend on shoreline access. Given the non-probability sample and retrospective accounts, conclusions concern perceived impacts rather than established causal effects.
